raw_text:
# Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Mechanics, and Guidelines

### Introduction and Mechanism of Action
Heart failure (HF) is a global public health challenge, historically managed by targeting neurohormonal overactivation, primarily the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) [1]. The therapeutic landscape shifted dramatically with the introduction of the first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), sacubitril/valsartan [2]. Sacubitril/valsartan exhibits a dual mechanism of action: it inhibits the neprilysin enzyme via its active metabolite sacubitrilat while simultaneously blocking angiotensin II type 1 ($\text{AT}_1$) receptors via valsartan [3]. Neprilysin is a zinc-dependent endopeptidase responsible for the degradation of several vasoactive peptides, including atrial natriuretic peptide, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), C-type natriuretic peptide, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [4]. By inhibiting neprilysin, sacubitril/valsartan augments these endogenous natriuretic peptides, thereby promoting vasodilation, natriuresis, diuresis, and antifibrotic and antihypertrophic effects [5]. Concomitantly, $\text{AT}_1$ receptor blockade prevents the adverse vasoconstrictive and sodium-retaining consequences of compensatory angiotensin II accumulation [6]. Early hemodynamic studies demonstrated that this dual neurohormonal approach lowers systemic vascular resistance and attenuates myocardial wall stress [7,8], independent of simple blood pressure lowering [9].

### Clinical Evidence in HFrEF
The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established the therapeutic superiority of sacubitril/valsartan over the standard-of-care angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor enalapril in patients with chronic heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF; left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF] $\leq 40\%$) [10]. The baseline characteristics of this cohort represented a typical chronic HF population [11]. Sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or first HF hospitalization by 20% compared with enalapril, while significantly mitigating clinical progression [12]. Mode-of-death analyses revealed that this survival benefit was driven by a robust reduction in both sudden cardiac death and death due to worsening heart failure [13]. Furthermore, patients treated with the ARNI reported significant, sustained improvements in health-related quality of life, assessed via the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) [14]. Secondary analyses also demonstrated a reduced risk of hyperkalemia during treatment with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) when combined with sacubitril/valsartan compared to enalapril [15].

### In-Hospital Initiation and Acute Management
Transitioning patients from acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) to maintenance therapy represents a critical clinical window. The PIONEER-HF trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan compared with enalapril in hemodynamically stabilized patients hospitalized for ADHF [16]. ARNI therapy achieved a significantly greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) at 8 weeks and reduced the risk of serious clinical events, such as rehospitalization. The TRANSITION trial corroborated these findings by showing that sacubitril/valsartan can be initiated safely and is similarly well-tolerated whether started pre-discharge or shortly after discharge [17]. Crucially, subgroup analyses from TRANSITION demonstrated that patients with newly diagnosed (*de novo*) HFrEF tolerated the drug exceptionally well, showing higher rates of target dose achievement and rapid biomarker improvement compared to patients with chronic disease [18].

### Advanced Heart Failure and Functional Outcomes
While the benefits of sacubitril/valsartan in mild-to-moderate HFrEF are clear, its role in advanced HF has been carefully scrutinized. The LIFE trial investigated sacubitril/valsartan versus valsartan alone in patients with advanced HFrEF (NYHA class IV symptoms and LVEF $\leq 35\%$) [19]. In this sicker cohort, ARNI therapy did not demonstrate superiority over valsartan in lowering NT-proBNP levels or improving clinical composites, highlighting the physiological limits of neprilysin inhibition due to severe downstream receptor blunting. Conversely, in chronic, ambulatory HFrEF, ARNI therapy has shown functional benefits. The OUTSTEP-HF trial compared sacubitril/valsartan with enalapril on submaximal exercise capacity, demonstrating a significant improvement in the 6-minute walk test distance at 12 weeks, although daily physical activity levels measured via accelerometry were comparable between groups [20]. Functional benefits were also seen in patients with chronic functional mitral regurgitation secondary to left ventricular dysfunction in the PRIME trial, which showed a significant reduction in the effective regurgitant orifice area and regurgitant volume [21].

### Sacubitril/Valsartan Across the LVEF Spectrum
Extending the benefits of neprilysin inhibition to patients with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF; LVEF $\geq 45\%$) was evaluated in the PARAGON-HF trial [22]. Sacubitril/valsartan narrowly missed its primary composite endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death [22]. However, pooled patient-level analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF demonstrated that the benefits of sacubitril/valsartan extend to patients with LVEF below the normal range (specifically up to 57%–60%) and are particularly pronounced in women [23]. The PARALLAX trial supported these observations by demonstrating that ARNI therapy significantly reduced NT-proBNP compared with individualized medical therapy in HFpEF, though it did not significantly improve submaximal exercise capacity [24].

### Cardiorenal Protection
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) frequently complicates HF management, creating a vicious cardiorenal cycle. The UK HARP-III trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan is safe and preserves kidney function in patients with moderate-to-severe CKD similarly to standard irbesartan therapy [25]. In heart failure, secondary analysis of PARADIGM-HF showed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly slows estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline compared with enalapril [26]. Similarly, significant renal protection was observed with ARNI therapy in the PARAGON-HF cohort, demonstrating its dual cardioprotective and nephroprotective profile across the ejection fraction spectrum [27].

### Guidelines and Clinical Practice
Based on this extensive trial evidence, clinical guidelines have firmly integrated sacubitril/valsartan into standard practice. The 2021 ESC Guidelines recommended sacubitril/valsartan as a replacement for ACE inhibitors/ARBs in symptomatic HFrEF [28]. The 2023 ESC Focused Update further emphasized the early, rapid optimization of GDMT [29]. Recent data from the PARAGLIDE-HF trial and subsequent pooled analyses have solidified ARNI's clinical utility in patients with HFmrEF or HFpEF following a worsening heart failure event [30]. Together, these studies highlight that early and comprehensive implementation of sacubitril/valsartan across the LVEF spectrum remains paramount to reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease and hospitalizations.
